habitat: Pallid bats inhabit arid and semi-arid regions of western North America, from British Columbia through the western United States to central Mexico. They frequent deserts, grasslands, shrublands, oak and pine forests, and agricultural areas. During the day, they roost in rock crevices, cliff faces, caves, mines, and occasionally buildings and bridges. They prefer vertical rock faces with narrow crevices that provide protection from predators and stable temperatures. They are residents — not migratory — in most of their range.
diet: Pallid bats have one of the most unique diets of any North American bat. While they eat some flying insects, they are specialized ground-gleaners — hunting large, ground-dwelling prey including scorpions, centipedes, crickets, beetles, grasshoppers, and even small lizards and mice. They are immune to scorpion venom, including that of the Arizona bark scorpion (the most venomous scorpion in North America). They detect prey using passive listening rather than echolocation, homing in on the sounds of prey moving on the ground, then swooping down to capture them.
behavior: Pallid bats are gregarious, roosting in colonies of 20-100 or more individuals during summer, typically in rock crevices. They emerge later than most bats, often well after dark, and fly low over the ground searching for prey with their exceptionally large ears. When prey is detected, they drop to the ground and capture it, then carry it to a perch to consume. They are gentle and have a musky odor described as similar to a skunk. Females give birth to 1-2 pups per year. Colonies relocate roosts frequently, sometimes every few days.
facts: Pallid bats have the largest ears relative to body size of any bat in North America. Their pale, cream-colored fur blends perfectly with the rocky desert environments they inhabit. They are one of the few bats known to prey on scorpions. Their immune system has evolved to neutralize scorpion venom without harm. Colonies are known to occupy the same roosts for decades. They have been observed visiting hummingbird feeders at night to drink sugar water. Pallid bats can live over 10 years in the wild.
naming: Pallid bat names might reflect their desert habitat, pale coloration, or scorpion-hunting prowess. Consider names like Dusty, Scorpio, Sahara, Gobi, Pale, Ghost, Sand, Phantom, Amber, Artemis (hunter goddess), Vesper (evening), or Dune.
